specStatements.text: Traditionally living things have been classified into groups depending on their structure and characteristics in a system developed by Carl Linnaeus.
Linnaeus classified living things into kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species. Organisms are named by the binomial system of genus and species.
Students should be able to use information given to show understanding of the Linnaean system.
Students should be able to describe the impact of developments in biology on classification systems.
As evidence of internal structures became more developed due to improvements in microscopes, and the understanding of biochemical processes progressed, new models of classification were proposed.

Due to evidence available from chemical analysis there is now a 'three-domain system' developed by Carl Woese. In this system organisms are divided into: Archaea (primitive bacteria usually living in extreme environments); Bacteria (true bacteria); Eukaryota (which includes protists, fungi, plants and animals).
Evolutionary trees are a method used by scientists to show how they believe organisms are related. They use current classification data for living organisms and fossil data for extinct organisms.

concepts.definition: The traditional system of classification, developed by Carl Linnaeus, in which living things are classified into groups depending on their structure and characteristics.

The groups Linnaeus classified living things into: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species. Kingdom is the largest group and species the smallest, so organisms placed in the same genus share more characteristics than organisms placed only in the same class.
The system used to name organisms, in which an organism is given a two-part name made up of its genus followed by its species, for example Panthera leo.

Classification systems proposed after Linnaeus. As evidence of internal structures became more developed due to improvements in microscopes, and the understanding of biochemical processes progressed, new models of classification were proposed.

The system developed by Carl Woese, due to evidence available from chemical analysis, in which organisms are divided into Archaea (primitive bacteria usually living in extreme environments), Bacteria (true bacteria) and Eukaryota (which includes protists, fungi, plants and animals).
A method used by scientists to show how they believe organisms are related, drawn using current classification data for living organisms and fossil data for extinct organisms.

misconceptions.question: In the binomial name Panthera leo, which Linnaean group does Panthera give?
misconceptions.correct: Panthera gives the genus, because the first part of a binomial name is the genus.
misconceptions.misconception: The first part of a binomial name gives a group larger than the genus, such as the family or the order.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that the two-part name places an organism in the Linnaean groups, but kingdom, phylum, class, order and family are more familiar words than genus, and 'family' sounds like a group of close relatives.
misconceptions.correction: Organisms are named by the binomial system of genus and species. The first part of the name gives the genus and the second part gives the species; family and order are separate, larger Linnaean groups.

misconceptions.question: In the binomial name Panthera leo, which part gives the species?
misconceptions.correct: The second part, leo, gives the species.
misconceptions.misconception: The first part of a binomial name gives the species and the second part gives the genus.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that the name is made of a genus and a species but not which comes first, and they assume the part shared by several organisms must be the species because a species is the group they meet most often.
misconceptions.correction: Organisms are named by the binomial system of genus and species, in that order: in Panthera leo the genus is Panthera and the species is leo.

misconceptions.question: Why were new models of classification proposed after the Linnaean system?
misconceptions.correct: Because better evidence about organisms became available from improved microscopes and from the understanding of biochemical processes.
misconceptions.misconception: New models of classification were proposed because scientists discovered large numbers of new species.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students think a classification system only has to change when there are more organisms to fit into it, rather than when new evidence about the organisms themselves becomes available.
misconceptions.correction: As evidence of internal structures became more developed due to improvements in microscopes, and the understanding of biochemical processes progressed, new models of classification were proposed.

misconceptions.question: In the three-domain system, are Archaea placed in the same domain as Bacteria?
misconceptions.correct: No. Archaea and Bacteria are two separate domains.
misconceptions.misconception: Archaea are true bacteria, so they are placed in the same domain as Bacteria.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Archaea are described as primitive bacteria and look similar to bacteria, so students treat the two as one group and do not realise the domains were separated using different evidence.
misconceptions.correction: Due to evidence available from chemical analysis, the three-domain system developed by Carl Woese divides organisms into Archaea (primitive bacteria usually living in extreme environments), Bacteria (true bacteria) and Eukaryota.

misconceptions.question: Which data do scientists use to draw an evolutionary tree?
misconceptions.correct: Current classification data for living organisms and fossil data for extinct organisms.
misconceptions.misconception: Evolutionary trees are drawn using fossil data only.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Evolutionary trees are usually met alongside work on fossils and extinction, so students assume every organism on the tree has been placed there using fossil evidence.
misconceptions.correction: Evolutionary trees are a method used by scientists to show how they believe organisms are related. They use current classification data for living organisms and fossil data for extinct organisms.

misconceptions.question: Which organisms are included in the domain Eukaryota?
misconceptions.correct: Protists, fungi, plants and animals are all included in Eukaryota.
misconceptions.misconception: Protists, fungi, plants and animals are each a separate domain of their own.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students have already met these as separate groups of organisms and assume the three-domain system simply renames those groups, so they list them alongside Archaea and Bacteria.
misconceptions.correction: In the three-domain system organisms are divided into Archaea, Bacteria and Eukaryota; Eukaryota is the domain which includes protists, fungi, plants and animals.

mcqs.stem: A student is given the names of two organisms: Panthera leo and Panthera pardus. Which Linnaean group is given by the shared name Panthera?

options.rationale: A student who believes the first part of a binomial name gives a group larger than the genus reads Panthera as one of those larger groups; order is a separate Linnaean group and is not used in the binomial system.

options.text: Their family in the Linnaean system
options.rationale: A student who believes a shared first name shows a family, because family sounds like a group of close relatives, picks this; in the binomial system the first part of the name gives the genus.

options.text: Their genus in the Linnaean system
options.rationale: Organisms are named by the binomial system of genus and species, so the first part of each name, Panthera, gives the genus that the two organisms share.

options.text: Their species in the Linnaean system
options.rationale: A student who believes the first part of a binomial name gives the species picks this; the species is given by the second part of each name, leo or pardus, so the two organisms are different species.

mcqs.stem: Linnaeus classified living things depending on their structure and characteristics. Why were new models of classification later proposed?

options.text: Because much larger numbers of species were discovered
options.rationale: A student who believes a classification system only changes when more organisms are found picks this; new models were proposed because better evidence about organisms became available, not because more species were counted.

options.text: Because improved microscopes showed internal structures
options.rationale: As evidence of internal structures became more developed due to improvements in microscopes, and the understanding of biochemical processes progressed, new models of classification were proposed.

options.text: Because fossils showed how organisms are related
options.rationale: A student who believes that relationships between organisms are shown by fossil data alone thinks fossils revealed how organisms are related and so drove the new models; in fact new models were proposed because improved microscopes and biochemical evidence revealed internal structures, and fossil data is only used for extinct organisms on evolutionary trees.

options.text: Because plants, animals and fungi each needed their own group
options.rationale: A student who believes protists, fungi, plants and animals are each a domain of their own thinks new models were proposed to give each of these groups its own separate place; in fact these are all included together within the single domain Eukaryota, and new models were proposed because better evidence about internal structures became available.

mcqs.stem: In the three-domain system developed by Carl Woese, into which three groups are organisms divided?

options.rationale: Due to evidence available from chemical analysis, organisms are divided into Archaea, Bacteria and Eukaryota, with protists, fungi, plants and animals included in Eukaryota.
A student who believes Archaea are true bacteria leaves out a separate Archaea domain and fills the gap with protists; Archaea form their own domain and protists are part of Eukaryota.
A student who believes protists are a domain of their own puts them in place of Eukaryota; protists are one of the groups included within the domain Eukaryota.
A student who believes animals are a domain of their own names them as the third group; animals are included in Eukaryota together with protists, fungi and plants.
